llm_response.content:
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

──────────────────────────────────────────  

1. Identification Strategy  
Chosen design: Classroom-level teacher-switching event study (difference-in-differences in an “event-study” framework) with an errors-in-variables IV refinement.

Rationale  
• Research question is whether the causal effect implied by a teacher’s value-added (VA) estimate is realized when new cohorts of students are exposed to that teacher.  
• Between 1989-2009 many teachers switch schools, grades, or exit the district. A switch creates a quasi-experiment for the incoming and outgoing cohorts within the same school-grade, holding calendars, curricula, principals, and peer groups largely constant.  
• Design follows Chetty-Friedman-Rockoff (2014) logic but is fully implementable with the information stated.  
• Step 1 (reduced form): Estimate leave-one-year-out VA for every teacher.  
• Step 2 (causal test): When a high-VA teacher replaces a low-VA teacher (or vice-versa), compare the change in average test scores in that school-grade-year to the change predicted by the VA difference. This is a DID: treated cohort = cohort after the switch; control = cohort before the switch in the same school-grade.  
• Step 3 (bias diagnosis): Instrument the contemporaneous VA of the classroom with the leave-one-year-out VA to address attenuation from estimation error and test for forecast bias (β̂ should equal 1 if VA is unbiased).  

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
Continuous: 𝑉𝐴_{jt} – the leave-one-year-out value-added estimate of the teacher (j) to whom student i is assigned in subject s and year t.  

Control / counterfactual  
Students in the same school × grade × year who are taught by a teacher whose VA differs from the focal teacher. The DID comparison uses cohorts in the same school-grade before and after the switch.  

Treatment timing / event definition  
An “event” occurs in year t when teacher j enters (or exits) school-grade g. Event time τ = 0 for the first year the new teacher teaches the cohort; τ = –1 is the last year with the old teacher; τ ∈ {–4,…,+4} used for event-study graphs.  

(We do not use an RDD because there is no naturally occurring cutoff, and IV is used only for measurement-error correction.)  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Switch exogeneity: The timing and destination of teacher moves are uncorrelated with shocks to student achievement in the affected school-grade. Plausibility: Urban districts typically reassign for seniority, leave, or budget shocks rather than specific cohorts; still testable with pre-trends.  
A2. Within-school-grade cohort equality: Conditional on observables, students are randomly assigned to classrooms inside a grade × year. Plausible given central timetabling; evaluate by balance tests on lagged scores/demographics.  
A3. No interference/spillovers between classrooms. Plausible for standardized tests that are teacher-specific; address via robustness excluding departmentalized grades.  
A4. Stable VA: A teacher’s true productivity is constant over short horizons (no large learning shocks). Reasonable across adjacent cohorts; can allow teacher × year random effects as robustness.  
A5. First-stage relevance & classical measurement error: Leave-one-year-out VA is a strong instrument for true current VA and the error is uncorrelated with student outcomes. Check F-statistic and implement split-sample VA to minimise mechanical correlation.  

4. Main Threats and Mitigations  
T1. Non-random teacher mobility (e.g., good teachers choose improving schools). Mitigation:  
• Include school × grade × year fixed effects in the event regressions so identification uses only within-school-grade changes.  
• Test for differential trends in −4,…,−1 years; failure to reject flat pre-trends supports exogeneity.  

T2. Sorting of students to high-VA teachers within schools. Mitigation:  
• Balance checks on lagged test scores and demographics across classrooms inside school-grade-year.  
• Estimate models with student fixed effects for multi-year panels (grades 4–8) to absorb any persistent unobserved ability.  

T3. Measurement error in estimated VA generating attenuation. Mitigation:  
• Use leave-two-year-out VA or split-sample VA as an IV for current VA (errors-in-variables IV).  
• Report both OLS and IV; compare coefficients to bound bias.  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data work
library(fixest)         # high-dim FE and IV
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data -------------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("district_panel_1989_2009.csv")   # one row per student-year-subject

# 2. Construct key variables ----------------------------------------------
# Prior achievement (one-year lag)
setorder(dt, student_id, year, subject)
dt[, lag_score := shift(test_score, 1, type = "lag"), 
   by = .(student_id, subject)]

# Teacher identifiers
dt[, teacher_year := interaction(teacher_id, year, drop = TRUE)]

# 3. Step-1: Estimate leave-one-year-out VA -------------------------------
# Collapse to teacher-year means (could also use EM algorithm)
teacher_means <- dt[!is.na(test_score), 
                    .(avg_gain = mean(test_score - lag_score, na.rm = TRUE)),
                    by = .(teacher_id, year, subject)]

# Leave-one-year-out VA
teacher_means[, va_est := (avg_gain - mean(avg_gain, na.rm = TRUE)),
              by = .(teacher_id, subject)]
# Merge back
dt <- merge(dt, teacher_means[, .(teacher_id, year, subject, va_est)], 
            by = c("teacher_id","year","subject"))

# 4. Step-2: Event-study DID specification -------------------------------
# Build event time around switches
# Identify first year teacher appears in school-grade
dt[, first_year := min(year), by = .(teacher_id, school_id, grade, subject)]
dt[, event_time := year - first_year]        # τ=0 for entry year

# Keep window [-4, +4]
dt <- dt[event_time >= -4 & event_time <= 4]

# Estimate: test score on teacher VA with rich FE
event_mod <- feols(test_score ~ i(event_time, va_est, ref = -1) |
                   school_id^grade^year + subject + lag_score,
                   data = dt, cluster = "school_id^grade")

# 5. Step-3: IV for measurement error -------------------------------------
iv_mod <- feols(test_score ~ 1 | school_id^grade^year + subject + lag_score | 
                va_est ~ va_est_split,
                data = dt, cluster = "school_id^grade")

# 6. Robustness: placebo on future VA -------------------------------------
dt[, future_va := shift(va_est, +1, type = "lead"), 
   by = .(teacher_id, subject)]
placebo_mod <- feols(test_score ~ future_va |
                     school_id^grade^year + subject + lag_score,
                     data = dt, cluster = "school_id^grade")
```

Key notes  
• `school_id^grade^year` generates saturated school×grade×year fixed effects.  
• `i(event_time, va_est)` interacts discrete event time dummies with VA to draw the event-study plot (coefficient βτ should be ~0 for τ<0 and ≈1 for τ≥0 if VA is unbiased).  

6. Expected Results  
Economic theory and prior evidence suggest that an increase of 1 student-level standard deviation in teacher VA raises contemporaneous student test scores by roughly 0.2–0.25 SD. If VA estimates are unbiased, the IV coefficient on VA should be close to 1. I expect small downward bias in OLS (β̂≈0.8) due to measurement error; after IV correction, coefficient should move toward 1.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Event-Study/DID)  
C1: Pre-trend (parallel trends) visually flat  1  
C2: No systematic sorting within school-grade⁠ 0.8  
C3: No interference/spillover across classes  0.7  
C4: Correct timing/no anticipation  1  
C5: Strong first-stage for IV (F>10)  1  

Overall, three of five items are clearly satisfied, two are plausible but warrant additional robustness checks and balance tests.
